note: Second carding pass, chosen after Siddharth tested the live UI and found answers thin where assets were registry-only. These are eBooks, whitepapers and the industry/solution one-pagers - short documents a rep sends to a specific buyer. Written from corpus/text/*.txt. The dominant finding is a stale-numbers problem the age rule alone would not catch: the 2020-vintage one-pagers all cite '500+ enterprise customers & 600,000+ active users' and brand the company 'AccOps', where current material says 800+ customers and 2M+ users. Sending one to a prospect undersells Accops by more than half, so stale_risk names the specific figures rather than just the year.

schema_notes.stale_risk: Why this document might mislead. For the 2020 one-pagers it is not vagueness about age - it is that the customer and user counts printed on them are now wrong by a factor of three.
schema_notes.client_actual: Real customer names printed in the document. Supabase only, never in a model prompt.

cards.title: How DaaS Can Help You Transform Your BFSI Operations (eBook)
cards.key_problem: BFSI organisations took a tactical, point-in-time approach to remote access during Covid, and are now carrying VPN and VDI deployments that were never chosen strategically - while user numbers keep compounding as financial inclusion widens.
key_outcomes: DaaS decouples sensitive data from the user's device into the data centre
Provisioned in hours or days rather than the weeks or months on-premise VDI takes
Consumption-based infrastructure, so on-premise capacity is reserved for core BFSI systems
Particularly suited to remote branch offices with no local IT staff
Removes break-fix work from branch users
cards.brief: A short buyer-education eBook arguing the case for cloud-hosted virtual desktops in banking, financial services and insurance. Its framing is post-Covid: the sector improvised its way through with VPNs and point VDI deployments, and now has the chance to choose deliberately. Four arguments follow - security and compliance through keeping data in the data centre rather than on the endpoint, faster time to value because a managed stack provisions in hours, on-demand infrastructure so that capex-heavy on-premise VDI is reserved for core operations, and relief for branch offices that have no IT staff to handle break-fix.
cards.use_for: An early-stage BFSI conversation with a CIO who has not yet decided between on-premise VDI and DaaS. Education, not a product pitch.
cards.stale_risk: Written in the immediate post-Covid period and argues from that moment ('the recent past', 'a Covid-hit business environment'). The reasoning holds but the framing is dated for a 2026 conversation.
cards.internal_reason: No public URL confirmed. Buyer-education content with no customer detail - a candidate for publication.

cards.title: Remote Browser Isolation: A Modern Approach to Modern Cyberthreats (eBook)
cards.key_problem: Signature-based endpoint security cannot stop polymorphic malware or an attacker who establishes presence before detection, so allowing scanned internet traffic into the corporate network still leaves it exposed.
key_outcomes: Runs the browser on a remote computer in an isolated network
Corporate network is never exposed to internet content
Effective against ransomware, zero-day and polymorphic malware
Removes cookie-based tracking and demographic profiling of staff
Argues multi-tiered endpoint security over perimeter-only strategy
cards.brief: The buyer-facing version of the browser isolation argument, covering the same reasoning as the ISA whitepaper in plainer language. It starts from why conventional models fail - signature-based antivirus cannot see polymorphic malware, and attackers establish presence before detection - then makes the case that the endpoint, not the perimeter, is where threats originate. Remote Browser Isolation is the answer offered: a virtual browser on a remote machine in an isolated network, so internet content never reaches the corporate network. It also covers website tracking and demographic profiling as a route to targeted attacks on staff.
cards.use_for: A CISO or IT head evaluating internet isolation who wants the argument before the product. Pairs with the Virtual Browser technical document for the same conversation at a deeper level.
cards.internal_reason: No public URL confirmed. No customer detail - a candidate for publication.
cards.pairs_with: sharepoint/Accops Virtual Browser Solution for Internet Access.pdf

cards.source: sharepoint/Accops - eBook - Biometric MFA & continuous monitoring for critical users.pdf
cards.title: Biometric MFA and Continuous Monitoring for Critical Users (eBook)
cards.key_problem: Identity protection was a minor concern while everyone worked from corporate PCs on office premises; with a distributed workforce, authentication is the first and most important line of defence, and passwords alone only prove someone knows a secret.
key_outcomes: Deloitte: 500,000 people affected by data breaches between February and May 2020
US government reported a 3,000% increase in identity theft attempts during Covid
Passwords prove knowledge, not identity - no defence against credential sharing
Facial authentication with continuous monitoring for high-assurance users
Aimed at BFSI, healthcare, pharma, government and PSUs as the regulated sectors
cards.brief: An eBook arguing that facial authentication and continual monitoring have become necessary rather than optional for critical users in a distributed workforce. It opens with the shift in security architecture - control over endpoints and premises is gone - and cites Deloitte and US government figures on the surge in identity theft during the Covid period as evidence that organisations moved to remote work faster than they hardened authentication. The core argument is that a passwords-only model grants access on 'what you know', so it cannot establish that the person logged in is the real user, which matters most in heavily regulated sectors handling sensitive data.
cards.use_for: A regulated-industry buyer questioning why MFA is not enough, or any conversation about continuous verification for privileged and critical users.
cards.stale_risk: The Deloitte and US government statistics are from the 2020 Covid period. Still true as history but they are no longer current evidence - check for newer figures before using them in a 2026 pitch.
cards.internal_reason: No public URL confirmed. No customer detail - a candidate for publication.

cards.title: Identity and Access Management: The Key to the Treasure Trove (Whitepaper)
cards.key_problem: IAM now has to cover employees, contractors, partners, remote users, customers, IoT devices, robots and APIs across multi-cloud hybrid estates, which is a far wider scope than the identity systems most enterprises actually built.
key_outcomes: Frames IAM as the building block for Authentication, Authorisation and Auditing (AAA)
Scope extends past people to IoT devices, robots, APIs and microservices
Covers SSO, two-factor, MFA and privileged access management as the component set
Positions IAM alongside DaaS, VDI, ZTNA and CASB rather than as a separate concern
Data governance so only necessary and relevant identity data is shared
cards.brief: A conceptual whitepaper on identity and access management as the foundation of enterprise security rather than a product category. It defines IAM as the mechanism that lets the right entities use the right resources at the right time, notes that AAA rests on it, and makes the point that identities are now assigned to non-human things - IoT devices, robots, APIs, microservices - as well as to employees, contractors, partners and customers. Systems covered are single sign-on, two-factor and multi-factor authentication, and privileged access management. It situates IAM within the wider remote-access stack of DaaS, VDI, ZTNA and CASB.
cards.use_for: A buyer who needs the IAM concept framed before a product discussion, or a procurement audience wanting the vocabulary. Vendor-neutral enough to send early.
cards.stale_risk: Argues from the Covid-era shift to hybrid work as the driving change, which dates the framing.
cards.internal_reason: No public URL confirmed. Conceptual content with no customer detail - a candidate for publication.

cards.title: Accops for Healthcare: A Single-Stop Cybersecurity Solution (Whitepaper)
cards.key_problem: A modern hospital is a loose conglomeration of digital systems - HIMS, LIMS, PACS, EMR/EHR, e-prescribing, remote patient monitoring, IoMT devices - each holding or moving patient data, and securing access across all of them is a different problem from securing one application.
key_outcomes: Maps the healthcare application estate: HIMS, LIMS, PACS, EMR/EHR, e-prescribing, RPM
Covers IoMT devices, infusion pumps, HVAC and radiology systems as attack surface
Argues one access layer across a fragmented clinical estate
Healthcare named as the most-targeted sector for data breaches
cards.brief: A healthcare-sector whitepaper whose useful contribution is the inventory: it enumerates the systems a typical hospital actually runs - hospital and laboratory information management, picture archiving, electronic medical and health records, e-prescribing, remote patient monitoring - plus decision support, intelligent HVAC, infusion pumps, radiology information systems and IoMT devices, and makes the point that each is a route to patient data. The argument that follows is for a single access and identity layer across that fragmented estate rather than per-system security.
cards.use_for: A hospital or healthcare provider conversation, particularly where the buyer is describing a fragmented clinical application estate. The system inventory is the reusable part.
cards.stale_risk: Opens with an extended topical hook about the Ukraine-Russia war and speculation over Vladimir Putin's health records. That framing has not aged well and reads oddly in 2026 - use the technical content and the system inventory, not the introduction.
cards.internal_reason: The opening section is a topical geopolitical hook that would not reflect well on Accops if sent to a customer today. Internal reference.

cards.title: Accops for Healthcare: Industry Solution One-Pager (2020)
cards.key_problem: Healthcare CIOs accelerating digital transformation face rising volumes of electronic health records and a sector that is first in line for cyberattack, while simultaneously absorbing Covid patient influx and telehealth demand.
key_outcomes: Positions Accops as a single-stop shop across remote access, VDI, MFA, SSO and thin clients
Cites DSCI recognition as the only Indian VDI provider named for work from home
Modular product set sized for businesses of any scale
cards.brief: A two-page industry one-pager for healthcare, structured as company positioning followed by sector challenges. The Accops pitch is breadth: one vendor for remote access, application virtualisation, VDI, MFA, identity federation, SSO and thin clients, modular enough to fit any size of organisation. The healthcare section covers digital transformation pressure, growing volumes of electronic health records, and the sector's exposure to data breaches.
cards.use_for: A quick leave-behind for a healthcare prospect - but check the figures first, they are five years out of date.
cards.stale_risk: Copyright 2020, brands the company 'AccOps' in the old style, and cites '500+ enterprise customers & 600,000+ active users'. Current material says 800+ customers and 2M+ users, so sending this UNDERSELLS Accops by more than half. The DSCI work-from-home recognition is also a 2020 reference. Do not send without updating the numbers.
cards.internal_reason: Figures are materially wrong in Accops' own disfavour. Internal until refreshed.

cards.title: Accops for Automotive Companies: Industry Solution One-Pager (2020)
cards.client: A named list of Indian automotive and industrial manufacturers, plus a defence research organisation
cards.client_actual: Force Motors, Bharat Forge, DRDO, HPCL, Polycab, Thermax, Yokohama, Yazaki, Sandhar
cards.key_problem: The automotive industry is in its biggest transformation in half a century - climate regulation, fast-changing rules, volatile economics and rapid technology change - and needs flexible, resilient IT for continuity, while remote work compounds existing infrastructure problems.
key_outcomes: Nine named automotive and industrial reference customers
Secure access to graphics workstations as well as business applications
Single vendor across remote access, virtualisation, VDI, MFA, SSO and thin clients
cards.brief: The automotive industry one-pager. It frames the sector as undergoing its largest transformation in fifty years and argues that resilient, flexible IT is now a continuity requirement rather than an efficiency question. The Accops positioning is the standard single-vendor breadth argument, with the sector-specific addition of secure access to graphics workstations alongside ordinary business applications. Its real value to a rep is the reference list: nine named Indian automotive and industrial manufacturers.
cards.use_for: An automotive or industrial manufacturing prospect, mainly for the named reference list. Numbers need updating before it leaves the building.
cards.stale_risk: Copyright 2020, old 'AccOps' branding, and cites '500+ enterprise customers & 600,000+ active users' against the current 800+ and 2M+. Sending it understates Accops substantially.
cards.internal_reason: Names nine real customers and carries figures that are now wrong. Internal reference only.

cards.title: Accops Remote Virtual Browser: Internet Isolation One-Pager (2020)
cards.client: A named list spanning Indian defence research, atomic energy, e-commerce, insurance, government and manufacturing, plus a Japanese prefecture
cards.client_actual: DRDO, IGCAR, Ibaraki Prefecture (Japan), Flipkart, LIC, NIC, HDFC Life, L&T, Tech Mahindra, Polycab
cards.key_problem: Internet applications and protocols were built to deliver business outcomes rather than to be secure, and security was retrofitted only once attackers began exploiting them - so endpoint and network defences are permanently a step behind.
key_outcomes: Ten named reference customers including defence and atomic energy
Remote virtual browser keeps internet content off the corporate network
Positioned for high-security environments rather than general enterprise
cards.brief: The internet isolation one-pager, and the shortest form of the browser isolation argument in the library. The reasoning is compressed from the eBook and the ISA whitepaper: internet protocols were never designed to be secure, defences are reactive by nature, so the answer is to keep browsing off the corporate network entirely via a remote virtual browser. Its distinguishing value is the reference list, which includes DRDO and IGCAR - defence research and atomic energy, the most security-sensitive customers Accops can cite.
cards.use_for: A high-security internet isolation conversation - defence, atomic energy, government - where naming comparable customers matters more than the technical argument.
cards.stale_risk: Copyright 2020, old 'AccOps' branding, and the '500+ customers / 600,000+ users' figures are now wrong against 800+ and 2M+.
cards.internal_reason: Names DRDO and IGCAR among ten real customers. Defence and atomic-energy references must not be forwarded.

cards.title: Accops Solution for Online Examinations and ICT Labs (2020)
cards.client: A named list of Indian and Japanese universities, schools and examination administrators
cards.client_actual: Kyoto University (Japan), IIT-Delhi, Ashoka University, KR Mangala World School, NSEIT, SEBI, Satvat Infosol, Ginger Webs
cards.key_problem: Academia moved to remote teaching almost overnight, but examinations - the part that determines students' futures and demands proper invigilation - remained hard to administer online at scale.
key_outcomes: Physical PC labs transformed into virtual on-demand ICT labs
Self-service portal so students and faculty reserve lab access themselves
Named users include Kyoto University, IIT-Delhi and Ashoka University
Exams administered to lakhs of government-job candidates via NSEIT and SEBI
cards.brief: The education one-pager, covering two related use cases: converting physical PC labs into virtual on-demand ICT labs with a self-service reservation portal, and administering high-stakes online examinations. The examination argument is the stronger one - it names NSEIT, SEBI, Satvat Infosol and Ginger Webs as having run exams for lakhs of government-job candidates on the platform, which is a scale claim few competitors can match in India. University references span India and Japan.
cards.use_for: An education or examination-body prospect, and the only asset covering HyLabs and the exam use case. The scale reference - lakhs of candidates - is the headline.
cards.stale_risk: Copyright 2020, old 'AccOps' branding, '500+ customers / 600,000+ users' now understated, and the Covid framing dates the argument.
cards.internal_reason: Names eight real customers including universities and examination bodies.

cards.title: Accops Access Modes: HyLite, Portal, Client and Reverse Proxy Compared
cards.key_problem: Accops publishes applications through several different access modes with different capabilities, and choosing the wrong one for a given application type produces a deployment that cannot support what the customer needs.
key_outcomes: Five publishable application types enumerated, from reverse-proxied web to client-server
HyLite mode is fully clientless but supports only virtual apps, RDP and reverse-proxied web
Digital Workspace Portal has three distinct modes of operation
Written as the reference for matching an access mode to an application type
cards.brief: An internal technical reference setting out every Accops access mode and what each can actually deliver. It first enumerates the five publishable application types - reverse-proxied web, tunnelled web, HyWorks virtual applications and desktops, Microsoft RDP connections, and client-server applications - then works through the access modes, notably the Digital Workspace Portal and its three operating modes. The important detail for a solution architect is that HyLite is entirely clientless but supports only a subset of application types, so an estate with client-server applications cannot be served by HyLite alone.
cards.use_for: A pre-sales or solution-design conversation where the question is which access mode fits the customer's application estate. Reference material, not a pitch.
cards.stale_risk: Dated 2020 and access-mode capabilities change between releases - verify against current documentation before designing to it.
cards.internal_reason: Marked 'Accops Confidential' in its own header.

cards.title: Accops ZTNA for Government
cards.key_problem: Government departments need to give employees, contractors and vendors access to internal applications without extending the network to them, and traditional VPN gives flat network access rather than per-application control.
key_outcomes: Zero Trust access to government applications without network-level exposure
Identity and device posture evaluated before access is granted
Agentless browser-based access as well as agent-based
Positioned for departmental and PSU deployments
cards.brief: The government-sector ZTNA deck, covering zero-trust access to departmental applications as a VPN replacement. It makes the standard ZTNA argument in a public-sector frame: identity and device posture verified before access, per-application rather than network-level permission, and both agentless and agent-based paths so contractors and vendors on unmanaged devices can be served. Overlaps substantially with the newer 'Accops Solutions for Government' reference architecture, which is more complete.
cards.use_for: A government ZTNA conversation. Prefer the 2026 'Accops Solutions for Government' reference architecture where a full architecture is wanted; use this for a ZTNA-only discussion.
cards.stale_risk: No date in the document. The 2026 government reference architecture covers the same ground more completely and is current.
cards.superseded_by: sharepoint/Accops Solutions for Govt. V1 '26.pdf - broader and dated 2026. Prefer it for a full architecture discussion.
cards.internal_reason: Government-sector positioning material. No public URL confirmed.

cards.title: Accops HySecure: Product Overview
cards.key_problem: A prospect hearing about HySecure for the first time needs a short description of what the gateway is and does, rather than the full datasheet's exhaustive capability list.
key_outcomes: Short-form description of the HySecure gateway and its role
Positions HySecure as the single entry point to corporate applications
Covers agent and agentless access at an overview level
cards.brief: A brief product overview of HySecure, written as the short introduction rather than the specification. It describes the gateway as the single controlled entry point into the corporate network for web, client-server, RDP and virtual applications, with agent and agentless access paths. The full capability detail lives in the HySecure datasheet; this exists for the moment in a conversation where that would be too much.
cards.use_for: A first-touch explanation of HySecure, or an internal briefing for someone new to the product. Use the current datasheet when the prospect wants specifics.
cards.stale_risk: Marked v1 with no date, and the public HySecure V5 2026 datasheet is the current source of truth on capabilities.
cards.superseded_by: public/Accops Hysecure Datasheet V5 2026.pdf - current, public and far more complete. Prefer it whenever specifics are needed.
